newsitem.title: BELGIUM: French rebate boosts European car sales.
newsitem.headline: French rebate boosts European car sales.

text.p: Soaring French demand for new cars before the end of a state incentives scheme led to a 12.2 percent jump in sales in western Europe in September, the European car manufacturers association, ACEA, said on Tuesday.

New passenger car registrations rose to 971,600 units in September, up from 865,600 in the same month last year, but ACEA said the French incentives had distorted the market and the prospects for the rest of this year and next did not look good.
So far this year, sales have risen by 6.7 percent to more than 10 million new cars in the 15-nation European Union plus Norway, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
September's growth was largely explained by a 85.7 percent jump in sales in France, while major European markets like Britain and Italy weakened.
James Rosenstein, director of communications at ACEA, said there had been a rush of buyers to take advantage of the French incentive scheme for new cars during its last month.

The French rebates, nicknamed "Juppettes" after French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, were introduced a year ago to shore up the market which was crumbling after a previous 17-month rebate scheme expired.
The new-cars-for-old rebate programme has buoyed French car sales, up by 13.6 percent in the first nine months of 1996.
"If you are removing the artificial incentives to the market, the underlying trend (in western Europe) is still not that good," Rosenstein said in an interview.
"We don't expect the end of the year to be good...and next year we don't expect good growth at all."
The industry body has revised up its forecast for the year to overall growth of more than four percent, but this is still below the increase in the first nine months of 1996.

The west European market has been recovering somewhat following the 16 percent drop in 1993 but is still not near its 1992 peak. "And nobody expects it to get back to that peak by the end of this century," Rosenstein said.

While French sales jumped in September, they declined by 1.4 percent in Britain and by 8.5 percent in Italy -- which like other European governments is raising taxes and cutting spending to qualify for the EU's single currency.
On a more positive note, sales rose strongly in smaller markets like Norway, Spain, Portugal, Finland and Ireland.
ACEA's figures suggested that Volkswagen was further strengthening its position as the continent's leading carmaker. Its market share climbed to 17.7 percent from 17.5 percent last year.
The Volkswagen group, which includes Audi, Seat and Skoda, saw new registrations of its cars rise by 12.9 percent.

France's PSA, which groups Peugeot and Citroen, also boosted its share of the west European market, to 13.2 percent from 11.5 percent. Its French rival Renault had a 34.5 percent jump in sales, its market share rising to 10.9 percent from 9.1 percent.

However, two U.S. giants -- Ford and General Motors -- both lost market shares, to 10.5 and 12 percent respectively, even though new registrations for the GM group, which includes Opel and Saab, rose 11.2 percent in September.
Japanese carmakers also lost market share, to 10.8 percent from 11.3 percent.
September appeared to be a disappointing month for up-market car brands Volvo, Alfa Romeo and Jaguar.
Volvo's new registrations fell by 4.9 percent, Alfa Romeo's by 26.9 percent and Jaguar's by 19.5 percent compared with the same month last year.
